keep: The idea is named in one line up front: drawn and added like a vector, but the angle is a moment in time, and as a complex number it can be divided.
The picture is the brief's: a still 3 kN pull beside a phasor that turns and traces its wave, with a freeze button, then three phase currents whose sizes are dragged at a star point.

Twelve screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10), ending with mixed puzzles (11, 12). Each brief misconception has a puzzle with its own wrong pick: the angle read as a direction (2), the sizes added (4, 10), two frequencies on one diagram (6), division done wrongly (8), the difference shortcut when all three differ (11), adding instead of taking away for the line voltage (12).
The course puzzle is answered with the numbers it asks for: 10, 10 and 4 A leave 6 A, not 24 A.
The clock analogy reproduces the main result: an angle between two hands that means a time, not a direction.
fix: Causal step skipped: why phasors add like forces at all. Say that two arrows turning together carry their nose-to-tail sum round with them, so the sum's height is the two heights added at every instant. That is also why one frequency is needed.
Causal step skipped: why different frequencies cannot share a diagram. Say a 150 Hz arrow turns three times as fast as a 50 Hz one, so the angle between them changes from instant to instant.

Causal step skipped: why the neutral carries the sum. Say what flows out on the lines must come back, so the neutral carries what the lines do not cancel. Then show the 6 A worked by parts, as the picture computes it.
Division is stated, not shown: give the rule, divide the sizes and take away the angles, and say what being a number gives a phasor that a vector lacks.

False absolute in the rule of thumb: 'never the sizes added' is false with one line loaded alone, where the neutral carries all of it. Replace it with the true cases: balanced cancels, two equal lines leave the difference from the third, one line alone sends it all back.
Brief shows only the effect (a readout jumping). Name the cause the picture shows: the nose-to-tail chain no longer closes, and its gap is the neutral current.

The ideal case is not named: say once that this is pure sine waves at one frequency, and that harmonics from real loads can add up in the neutral. Put the same in ignores, with the rms and peak scaling of the arrows.

Practice lacks the safe way first, the taking-away and dividing steps, the quarter check on the angle, and the mistakes the puzzles catch (difference shortcut, reading the angle as a direction, adding for the line voltage, multiplying phasors for power).
Analogy breaks too thinly and does not show frequency: add that a clock with a faster movement drifts away, as two frequencies do, and that clock hands never add while phasors do.
numbers and sources are empty: list every number with its kind, and copy sources 1, 3, 4 and 5 from RESEARCH.
